title: OPP training questioned
article: Two Ontario Provincial Police officers involved in the fatal shooting of an Ottawa-area man in Forthton in July reasonably believed their lives were in danger, the province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) has concluded.

But while the civilian agency cleared the two officers of any wrongdoing in the shooting death, SIU director Ian Scott's report also raises potential questions about the officers' training and notes the officers did not provide statements in the probe.
An OPP spokesman said the force will now conduct its own investigation, as it always does after an SIU probe.
The two officers, whom the OPP and SIU are not naming, remain on duty and are relieved by the decision, said OPP Sgt. Kristine Rae.
"Once the investigation is completed, it's always a relief for anybody," she said.

The SIU, a civilian agency that investigates deaths or serious injuries involving police, said in a prepared statement it has concluded that "there are no reasonable grounds to believe two Ontario Provincial Police officers with the Leeds County Detachment committed any criminal offence in relation to the firearm death of a Hammond man in July 2009."
Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau, 35, of Hammond in Prescott- Russell, died in a confrontation with police at Forthton on the night of Friday, July 3.
Charbonneau was fatally shot after he allegedly struck an OPP officer with his pickup truck.
The SIU assigned five investigators and three forensic investigators to probe the incident.
The agency's statement provides a more detailed description of how the incident unfolded.
On the evening of July 3, it notes, officers conducting a RIDE program on Highway 401 at the off-ramp to Stewart Boulevard in Brockville told Charbonneau to pull his black pickup truck over.
Charbonneau did not properly identify himself and the officer smelled alcohol on his breath, said the SIU.
Charbonneau then fled north on County Road 29, involving officers in a pursuit that reached speeds of up to 150 km/h, the statement adds.
Charbonneau ran a red light at Centennial Road and drove around two civilian vehicles on the shoulder of the roadway, and at one point, an oncoming car was forced off the road, it adds.
About 6.7 kilometres into the chase, police deployed a spike belt, puncturing the front tires of the truck, but Charbonneau iving on, said the SIU.
Police responded with a "rolling block," a tactic used to slow a vehicle down by surrounding it on all sides.
"Mr. Charbonneau rammed the police vehicles in front of his truck in an attempt to escape the rolling block," adds the SIU statement.
"When the officer directly in front of Mr. Charbonneau applied his brakes, the truck was forced to stop approximately 13.3 kilometres north of Highway 401."
At that point, there were six police vehicles surrounding Charbonneau's truck, it adds.
There was a gap between two of the police cars and Charbonneau started ramming the vehicles directly behind and in front of him in an attempt to escape through that gap.
"A number of the officers had exited their vehicles" by then, adds the SIU.
"One of the subject officers ran toward the area of the left front corner of the pickup truck and used his baton to smash the front windshield.
The second subject officer approached the pickup truck with his gun drawn and smashed the driver's side window with his baton.
Many of the officers were shouting the police challenge, which Mr. Charbonneau ignored."
Charbonneau ram the police vehicles blocking him, and eventually created enough space to start pointing his truck toward the gap, said the statement.
"During the vehicle's last movement forward toward the opening, the two subject officers discharged their firearms at Mr. Charbonneau a total of eight times.
One of the bullets went through the driver's side mirror and struck Mr. Charbonneau in the head, killing him instantly."
According to Scott, there are two issues that can't be determined.

"First, due to the nature of bullet projectiles from the two identical police issue hand guns, it is impossible to determine which of the two subject officers discharged which bullets and therefore which officer was responsible for causing the death of Mr. Charbonneau," Scott is quoted as saying.

Second, notes Scott, because the pickup truck was moving forward at the time and ving forward after the fatal shot, "it is impossible to ascertain the exact location of the subject officers at the critical moments.
"The problem of their positioning at the critical moment is further exacerbated by the fact that they were moving both before and after discharging their weapons," added Scott.
"Neither subject officer provided a statement to the investigators, making it even more difficult to determine their precise location at the critical moment."
SIU spokesman Monica Hudon said the two subject officers were not interviewed by the agency.
Under the law, she said, subject officers are not required to be interviewed and do not have to submit their notes.
The police, said Scott, had the right both to stop Charbonneau when he refused to co-operate at the RIDE check and to pursue him when he bolted.
The suspect was "driving in a dangerous manner and he represented a threat to public safety," so the use of a rolling block was appropriate, he adds.
"Once the rolling block had been completed, the officers had reasonable grounds to arrest Mr. Charbonneau for dangerous driving at the minimum," notes Scott.
"They also had reasonable grounds to believe he would use any means necessary to continue fleeing from them."

"In my view, it is a reasonable conclusion for the subject officers to draw that the driver would have been prepared to run over anybody in the way in an attempt to escape through the gap," Scott also says.
However, the director's statement significantly makes a passing reference to a potential issue with the officers' training.

"The fact that officers were in the way of the truck when it likely would be driven in such a deliberately reckless manner raises significant training issues, but those issues are largely irrelevant to the question at hand: Did the subject officers reasonably perceive that they were in imminent threat of death or grievous bodily harm caused by the actions of Mr. Charbonneau?"
Scott answers "yes," both to that question and to the question of whether the officers reasonably believed the suspect's actions "were about to cause immediate and serious injury to another person."
"Whichever subject officer fired the lethal shot was standing at such an angle to the pickup truck that it was almost directly in front of him and reasonably capable of running him over," says Scott.

"The other subject officer was also justified in shooting at the driver, even though the shots were not lethal, to prevent the commission of an offence that would likely cause immediate and serious injury to another person.
Accordingly, each subject officer was justified in shooting at Mr. Charbonneau for different reasons, and it does not matter for the purposes of criminal liability which one fired the fatal shot."
Rae would not speak directly to the issue of officer training raised in Scott's statement.

"The OPP have launched an investigation pursuant to Section 11 of the Police Services Act that's required after the SIU completes their investigation, to review policy and the conduct of its police officers," Rae said Thursday.
"The whole incident will be reviewed."
Rae did not know specific details of the timing of that internal investigation.
